content: I hire maintenance apprentices and want better evidence and a better candidate experience. We train the procedures after hiring. Our current question is: You would always ask the supervisor before doing anything, right? I then mark anyone who hesitates as weak. Coach me and help me build a 30-minute interview. Ask one question at a time if you need anything.

Your current question supplies the answer you want, and marking hesitation as weakness measures response style rather than an apprentice’s judgment. Someone may pause because they are thinking about when clarification is necessary. Since you teach the procedures after hiring, assess entry-level learning, careful observation, and recognition of limits rather than knowledge of your site’s procedures.

Replace the question with: “You are given an unfamiliar task and part of the instruction is unclear. Talk me through what you would do next and why.” A neutral follow-up is: “What would you need to know before proceeding?” Record the proposed action and rationale; do not score how quickly they agree with you. A vague answer means evidence is missing, not automatically that ability is weak. We should have your trade specialist check any technical safety criteria before using them.

A workable first draft for 30 minutes is:

| Minutes | Purpose |
|---|---|
| 0–3 | Explain the agenda, note-taking, thinking time, and that school, home projects, volunteering, or work examples are welcome. |
| 3–10 | One example of learning an unfamiliar task, including how the candidate checked their understanding. |
| 10–17 | One example of noticing an error or mismatch and what they did about it. |
| 17–23 | The unfamiliar-task scenario above, with neutral follow-ups about information and limits. |
| 23–28 | Candidate questions, including training and supervision. |
| 28–30 | Explain the actual next steps and close. |

We will build common questions and task-specific anchors around the real entry requirements. Before the interview, candidates should receive the duration, format, assessed areas, preparation expectations, and a way to request access arrangements. During it, protect their question time and allow a pause without penalty.

To make the guide fit your work: what is one ordinary task a new maintenance apprentice would learn during their first month?

In month one they log observations from supervised visual checks and learn how to compare them with the task sheet. They must report mismatches and cannot authorize repairs. I want a usable question, neutral probes, scoring anchors and a short practice exercise for me. I also need to know how to handle a candidate who pauses before answering.

Use the interview to assess whether an apprentice can notice, record, and communicate a mismatch while recognizing their authority limits. Your month-one task gives us a concrete scenario without requiring procedures you intend to teach.

Keep the 30-minute agenda above. Use this as the six-minute scenario at minutes 17–23; retain the two earlier experience questions to collect actual examples of learning and checking work.

**Common question**

“You are an apprentice doing a supervised visual check. You are learning to log observations and compare them with a task sheet. You notice something that does not match the sheet. Your role requires reporting mismatches, and you cannot authorize repairs. Talk me through what you would do next and why.”

Stating these boundaries gives every candidate the information needed to reason about the task. Repeating them alone is not evidence of practical competence. This is a discussion of judgment, not a test of repair or isolation procedures.

**Neutral probes**

Use these only where the answer leaves the relevant evidence unclear. Give comparable opportunities across candidates and record which probes you used.

- Observation: “What would you record about what you noticed?”
- Comparison: “How would you explain the difference between the observation and the sheet?”
- Handoff: “What information would you include when reporting it?”
- Uncertainty: “What would you do if you were unsure whether it was a mismatch?”
- Limits: “Which decisions would be yours, and which would belong to someone else?”

Do not follow a vague answer with “You would tell the supervisor and avoid repairs, right?” That supplies the content rather than eliciting it. Do not demand invented technical details; refer questions about the site’s actual procedure to the responsible trade specialist.

**Provisional scoring anchors**

Rate each criterion separately, using notes from the answer. These authored anchors need a check by your supervisor or trade specialist before live use.

| Criterion | Limited evidence | Adequate evidence for this discussion | Strong evidence for this discussion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accurate observation and comparison | Says “something is wrong” without identifying what needs describing or comparing, after a neutral probe. | Describes recording the observed condition and the relevant mismatch with the task sheet. | Also distinguishes observation from assumption and explains how they would clarify an ambiguous comparison without guessing. |
| Reporting and handoff | Says they would “mention it” but leaves the recipient or useful content unclear after probing. | Reports the mismatch to the designated supervisor/responsible person and identifies the relevant observation and task-sheet reference. | Also explains how they would check that the report was understood and record any instruction received. |
| Recognition of limits | Leaves the boundary between reporting and repair decisions unclear after probing. | Explains that they can observe, log, and report but cannot authorize repairs. | Also identifies when uncertainty requires clarification and explains how they would seek direction rather than assume authority. |

Use **not demonstrated** when you have no relevant evidence—for example, you ran out of time or did not resolve a misunderstood question. That is separate from a limited response after a fair opportunity. Record an explicit proposal to authorize repairs despite the stated restriction as **contradictory evidence on the authority criterion**; do not average it away with polished communication. Equally, missing detail is not proof of unsafe behavior. These ratings inform accountable human review; they do not certify practical competence or make the hiring decision.

**When a candidate pauses**

Allow thinking time without filling the silence or marking it down. You can say, “Take a moment; you can also ask me to repeat or clarify the question.” If they need clarification, repeat the scenario or explain its wording without suggesting a course of action. If they still cannot answer, offer the same documented neutral probe opportunity you would offer anyone else, then record what was and was not demonstrated. Score the reasoning they provide, not speed, fluency, or the pause itself. Accommodations can change the mechanics while preserving the capability assessed.

**Your practice exercise**

We will practise elicitation first, then rating. Here is a fictional candidate response:

“I’d sort it out, I suppose. I’m usually good at spotting things.”

Give me just one neutral follow-up that would obtain useful evidence without supplying the action you hope to hear.
I would ask: You would report it to the supervisor and not touch anything, wouldn't you? I think that helps them understand what we mean.

It helps them identify your preferred answer, but it prevents you from finding out what they would propose. “Report it to the supervisor” supplies the action, and “wouldn’t you?” invites agreement. “Not touch anything” also adds a blanket rule beyond the authority restriction we established; the task permits supervised observations and logging, while repair authority is restricted.

Clarifying the task and coaching the answer are different. You can restate the supplied facts—“Your role is to observe, log, and report mismatches; you cannot authorize repairs”—if the candidate misunderstood them. Then ask for their reasoning without supplying a sequence. Record that clarification was given.

For the vague response “I’d sort it out,” try: “What would ‘sort it out’ involve in this situation?” That invites a concrete account without telling them the next action. If they then provide useful evidence, recognize it; do not keep probing mechanically.

This attempt still used a leading probe, so neutral elicitation is not yet demonstrated. We can make the next retry smaller: respond to the same vague candidate answer with one open question, without naming a desired action. What would you ask?

My retry: What would sorting it out involve in this situation? If the candidate then says they would record the observation and task-sheet reference, report it to the assigned supervisor and ask what to do if unsure, how should I record that evidence? Please finish with a concise debrief and stop our practice.

Your retry asks for concrete action without supplying it. You have demonstrated a neutral probe in this coached retry; because it closely follows the example I supplied, independent transfer remains untested.

Record the hypothetical candidate response as proposed action, not observed workplace performance:

| Field | Example record |
|---|---|
| Question/probe | Core mismatch scenario; neutral probe: “What would sorting it out involve in this situation?” |
| Evidence | Candidate proposes recording the observation and task-sheet reference, reporting to the assigned supervisor, and asking for direction if unsure. |
| Observation/comparison | Adequate evidence of relevant logging/reference information. How they describe the actual mismatch remains unspecified. |
| Reporting/handoff | Adequate for this discussion: identifies the recipient and useful information to report. Confirmation of receipt or understanding was not demonstrated. |
| Limits/uncertainty | Seeking direction when unsure is demonstrated. Explicit recognition that they cannot authorize repairs was not demonstrated in this response; it is not contradicted either. |
| Assistance | Response followed a neutral probe; scenario supplied reporting and authority boundaries to all candidates. No answer-bearing hint in this retry. |
| Limits of inference | Hypothetical reasoning only. Accuracy in a real check and practical competence remain untested. |

Do not mark this candidate weak for pausing, or infer repair authorization from an omission. If that boundary needs clarification in a live interview, use the planned neutral probe, “Which decisions would be yours, and which would belong to someone else?” Record their answer before rating that criterion. Rate independently before panel discussion and retain the evidence behind any disagreement.

Debrief: You changed an answer-bearing prompt into a neutral request for evidence. Keep the 30-minute structure, protect candidate question time, allow thinking time, and use criterion-specific notes rather than hesitation as a rating. The remaining preparation is to have the responsible trade specialist check the task and anchors before live use. We are stopping practice here.
